r: The course applies a sociological lens to tourism, examining its social construction, developmental impacts, and intersections with environment, ethnicity, class, gender, and technology. These are informational and analytical tasks — synthesizing readings, explaining social theory, and evaluating case studies of destination impact. Task-exposure research finds writing and analytical synthesis positively associated with exposure while critical-thinking evaluation resists it more, and this survey course sits closer to descriptive synthesis, a category AI already handles competently. Observed-usage data shows Computer and Mathematical work as the largest usage category, with writing tasks close behind, suggesting near-term augmentation of the course's paper and discussion work. Still, the binding constraint is institutional: the General Studies Social and Behavioral Sciences and Global Diversity designation places the course inside the gtPathways statutory transfer core. At 24 months realized classroom deployment remains limited and the gen-ed mandate holds the course in place. Rating Low, driven principally by institutional lock-in.

By 2031, AI will fluently produce sociological analysis of tourism's social impacts, ethnic and gender dimensions, and technology's role in the industry, substantially automating the descriptive-synthesis work that anchors the course's assignments. Task-exposure research classifies this kind of explanatory writing among the more exposed categories, and productivity studies on professional writing show large time savings alongside quality gains, meaning students could increasingly rely on AI to generate the very analysis this course teaches them to produce. What is not automated is the gtPathways Social and Behavioral Sciences and Global Diversity mandate: the course remains required transfer credit regardless of how automatable its content generation becomes. The rating rises to Medium — execution of sociological synthesis is broadly automatable, but the general-education requirement and the value of a student's own comparative literacy about tourism's social effects keep the course instrumentally anchored across a catalog cycle.

A decade out, AI produces sophisticated sociological analysis of tourism's global impacts on demand, and the descriptive and explanatory rationale for the course's core assignments is substantially eroded. Diffusion research cautions that adoption still lags capability considerably, but on a ten-year horizon this gap is less binding than at five years. What persists is the gtPathways general-education mandate, which in the central case continues to require a Social and Behavioral Sciences and Global Diversity course, and the residual value of a student's own capacity to evaluate AI-generated claims about tourism's social construction and ethical dimensions. The rating holds Medium, capped by the transfer requirement rather than by task difficulty. The genuine uncertainty concerns how such gen-ed courses are taught under ubiquitous AI, not whether the institutional requirement itself persists, which in the central case it does.
TTM 1600.d: Students examine tourism through a sociological lens enabling them to understand the way tourism is socially constructed, the social impacts of tourism development, the development of travel in modern society, and tourism as a global industry. Students focus on how tourism intersects with topics such as the environment, ethnicity, social-class, gender, and the role of technology.

r: The applied work is planning, scripting, and physically leading a half-day narrated walking tour of the Denver metro area, with students simulating professional tour guides and dining-experience hosts for real audience participants. This is embodied, real-time, in-person performance — storytelling delivery, live audience management, and improvisational adaptation — squarely in the categories task-exposure research classifies as low-exposure and that observed-usage data shows are least represented in current AI usage. AI can help draft narrative scripts or research cultural sites, but it cannot lead a live group through Denver streets, read audience engagement, or manage the logistics of a moving public event. No general-studies designation applies, and no licensure constraint binds, so institutional lock-in is weak; the protection here is entirely embodiment. At 24 months the instrumental need to physically practice tour-leading is untouched. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI-assisted itinerary generation, script drafting, and multimedia self-guided tour apps will be considerably more capable and more widely diffused, competing at the margins with human-led narrated tours for casual travelers. That erodes some of the planning-and-content rationale underlying the course. But the specific competence this course certifies — leading a live group, adapting a narrative to real-time audience reactions, coordinating a moving public event with dining logistics — remains an embodied, interpersonal skill that a chatbot or app does not perform. Verification burden is modest, but presence is not; the dampener from low embodiment holds the rating down even as planning tasks automate. The rating stays Low: capability growth in tour-content generation does not substitute for the practiced act of physically guiding people, which is what the course exists to teach.

A decade out, AI-driven tour-guide apps and personalized multimedia narration could meaningfully substitute for some human-led tourism in self-directed contexts, and capability trends suggest audio and interactive guide products will be materially better by 2036. This is a genuine long-horizon uncertainty for the tour-guide labor market broadly. Yet the course's specific applied task — a student physically organizing and leading a group walking tour with live audience participation — remains embodied and interpersonal in a way that resists direct substitution even as adjacent products improve; task-exposure research continues to place real-time in-person performance among the least automatable activities. No institutional lock offsets this, but none is needed. The rating holds Low, hedged by real uncertainty over how much self-guided AI tourism displaces human-guided tourism as a market, without displacing the instrumental value of learning to lead one.
TTM 4800.d: Tourism is all about stories. The art of creating and telling enlightening stories that reveal hidden and little known cultural treasures is the focus of this course. Students apply the theories and techniques of planning, leading, and managing a narrated walking tour for inbound tourists through a practical and hands-on learning experience. Students work in teams to organize a half-day narrated tour in the Denver metropolitan area on a weekend at the end of the semester. A team simulates being professional tour guides while the rest of the students simulate being the inbound tourists. Walking tours include audience participation and dining experiences.
